newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Election seen unlikely to derail NZ economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Election seen unlikely to derail NZ economy.

text.p: New Zealand's economy, in its strongest shape for decades and currently rated one of the world's most robust, is unlikely to be derailed by Saturday's general election, analysts say.

Few countries can match growth averaging over three percent for three years, core inflation around 2.5 percent, growing budget supluses coupled with tax cuts and debt repayment, a rising currency and stable unemployment of around six percent.

Bewildered by polls showing that economic success is not enough, Prime Minister Jim Bolger has warned New Zealanders to weep at the prospect of a "Sunday, bloody, Sunday" if the centre-left wins the election. He has predicted the "crash of '97" and a roll-back of 12 years of free-market reform.

But few analysts subscribe to the doom scenario and financial markets have only in recent days registered any pre-election jitters. The kiwi dollar has fallen nearly one U.S. cent -- but from an eight-year high hit last week.
The share market jumped to a 2-1/2 year high on Monday and long-bond yields have fallen a percentage point since June.
Most damning to Bolger's argument have been comments from international credit-rating agency Standard & Poor's that it saw no threat to New Zealand's AA+ sovereign credit rating.

Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers agreed with Bolger that changes to the central bank framework and labour market law, buy-backs of former state assets and limits imposed on foreign investment would be a "worrisome development".
But he said last week: "From our standpoint that seems to be relatively unlikely."
S&P believes future New Zealand governments under a new proportional system called MMP will be pulled towards centrist economic positions, as exerience elsewhere has shown.
Beers said the economy was as sound as it had been for years, and projected budget surpluses would cushion the impact of greater spending.

Treasury is also upbeat. "The economic and fiscal outlook for the next four years remains positive, with robust output and ongoing employment growth, and a fiscal position of substantial operating surpluses and risking net worth," it said last month.
The independent Reserve Bank was less bullish but still painted a bright picture, forecasting 2.0 percent real growth in the March 1997 year rising to 2.4 percent in 1998.

Polls predict a tight race but lean towards the three parties of the left. If correct, Labour, backed by the nationalist New Zealand First Party and supported by the left-wing Alliance, will take power with Helen Clark at the helm and the economically "dry" Michael Cullen as finance minister.
Clark moved to reassure investors on Tuesday, saying Labour, not its junior partners, would control a centre-left government and Cullen was the sole candidate for finance minister.

Markets fear the Alliance's plans to substantially increase spending to make all health and education free and NZ First's desire to curb foreign ownership in what is currently one of the world's most open economies.
Labour promises to spend more in health and education, to be paid for by scrapping National's second round of tax cuts.
Bankers Trust New Zealand chief economist David Plank said one of the few certainties of the election outcome is that social spending will rise, irrespective of who wins.

Labour would widen the Reserve Bank's inflation target band to -1 to 3 percent from 0-2 percent but with the Reserve Bank predicting inflation will rise to 2.7 percent in the September year, economists say Labour's band is effectively in place.
Labour has said it would reject its prospective partners' desire to widen the bank's target to include growth and employment, which the markets would find more disturbing.

A Reuters poll of 10 bankers, fund managers, stockbrokers and economists listed slower repayment of public debt, a wider Reserve Bank target and a significant rise in government spending as the likeliest policy changes after the election.

While most market watchers have been blase about prospects of a centre-left win, Bancorp Treasury Services Executive Director Roger Kerr said: "The market's apparent comfort with the Labour Party victory is somewhat of a myth."
The currency and bond markets had been blinded by a huge influx of capital -- over NZ$5 billion this year -- attracted by the highest real interest rates in the world, he said.

"Watch out for some wild fluctuations and volatility immediately after Saturday as the markets have a wake-up call on the realities of who may be playing power-broker in the formation of the first MMP-elected government," Kerr said.
